sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
William Langson Lathrop
(American, 1859-1938)
Early October
oil on canvas laid to masonite
signed W L LATHROP (lower right)

40 x 36 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Housed in a Bernard Badura frame. Exhibited: Hempstead, Long Island, New York, The Emily Lowe Gallery, Hofstra University, November 14, 1981 – January 3, 1982.Doylestown, Pennsylvania, James A. Michener Art Museum, The Painterly Voice Bucks County's Fertile Ground, October 21, 2011 – April 1, 2012. Lot Note:Lathrop did more than any other painter to make the Delaware Valley a destination for American artists. The present lot, Early October, is precisely the kind of painting that attracted them. The canvas is large and nearly square, and it is given over almost entirely to a stand of maples at the height of their fall color. The sky is reduced to a few small patches of pale blue at the upper edges, so the viewer stands inside the woods rather than in front of a view. Lathrop builds the foliage from a narrow range of related hues (copper, vermilion, and burnt orange), warmed with touches of yellow-green at right, and he keeps the paint soft and feathery where his Bucks County neighbors often preferred a more insistent touch. The effect is closer to the tonal, poetic landscape of his early career than to the brighter, more broken color of the Impressionists who followed him to New Hope. Slender trunks rise through the canopy without any clear horizon to anchor them, and the only human note is a pair of small animals grazing in the clearing, set among boulders that catch the low light. These details give the picture its scale and its stillness. Lathrop had a gift for the quiet, enclosed corner of the countryside, and he understood that October in the Delaware Valley is as much about atmosphere as about color. Pictures of this size and ambition are especially sought after among the artist's works, and Early October shows him giving the subject the room it deserves.

sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
Edward Willis Redfield
(American, 1869-1965)
Village Street
oil on canvas
signed E W REDFIELD (lower left)

26 x 20 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Housed in a Frederick Harer frame.Provenance:Jim’s of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey.Acquired from the above, July 2018.Lot Note:In Village Street, Redfield turns from open landscapes and river views to the close quarters of a Bucks County lane in late autumn. A tall tree, its crown still thick with orange and ochre leaves, rises almost to the top of the canvas and dominates the scene, while a narrow road slips beneath it toward a cluster of pale houses and a green-roofed porch. The sky is a hard, clear blue, and the paint is applied in the short, loaded strokes that characterize his mature work: flecks of amber for the foliage, hatched violet and gray for the shadows lying across the road, and a few quick notes of red along the branches at right. Redfield was committed to painting directly from nature in a single sitting, and the present lot has the immediacy that method produces, with the tangle of bare twigs, the slanting light, and the figure in pink at the far end of the street all recorded at speed and with certainty. A telephone pole stands among the trees at right, an unsentimental detail that places the scene firmly in the working life of an early twentieth-century village and suggests an artist more interested in what he saw than in making it picturesque. The view is tightly cropped and tall in format, and its upward thrust gives the foliage a monumentality out of proportion to its modest setting. It is an accomplished example of the artist's village subjects, painted with economy and conviction.
provenance: Jim’s of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey. Acquired from the above, July 2018.

description_block:
Walter Emerson Baum
(American, 1884-1956)
Sledding in Winter, 1946
oil on canvas
signed W E BAUM (lower right); signed again, titled, dated, and inscribed Painted for Woman's Auxiliary, Allentown Art Museum (on the reverse)

30 x 36 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Lot Note:Sledding in Winter belongs to the long run of snowbound village views that occupied Baum for decades. Born in Sellersville, he spent his career within miles of the subjects he painted, and he treated the town as a body of work to be returned to rather than a motif to be exhausted. Where contemporaries like Redfield pursued the sweep of the river and the weather, Baum was drawn to the settled community: the stone farmhouse, the painted clapboard, the red barn, and the road that connects them. The present lot is dated 1946, well into his maturity, and demonstrates the palette and confident handling he had by then made his own, with the snow built up as a tangible surface rather than a pale ground. The lone boy dragging a sled gives the scene its title and a modest narrative note, a kind of incident Baum favored over grand effects, and the artist's signature, lettered on the mailbox at the lower right, adds a wry touch in keeping with the scene's easy humor. His help to establish Allentown's Baum School of Art made him a teacher and civic figure as much as a painter, and works like this one reflect that rootedness, painted by someone who knew the place and its people.
provenance: Painted for Woman's Auxiliary, Allentown Art Museum
subject_matter: village, houses, snow, boy, sled, trees, road, sky, clouds, barn

description_block:
Edward Willis Redfield
(American, 1869-1965)
Winter on the Farm (Farbotnik Farm), c. 1935-1940
oil on canvas
signed E W REDFIELD (lower left); inscribed, titled, and dated (on the stretcher) 

32 x 40 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance:Jim’s of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey.Acquired from the above, 2004.Exhibited:Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, Annual Art Exhibition, 1944, no. 9.Princeton, New Jersey, The Gallery at Bristol-Myers Squibb, Up the River: The Pennsylvania Impressionists and Modernists, New Jersey, October 1 – November 25, 2001.Literature:John W. Fletcher, Edward Willis Redfield 1869-1965, An American Impressionist: His Paintings and the Man Behind the Palette, Lahaska, Pennsylvania, 1996, p. 196, no. 1058 (as Winter on the Farm).Brian Peterson, Up the River: The Pennsylvania Impressionists and Modernists, Princeton, 2001, p. 25, illustrated.John M. W. Fletcher, Edward Willis Redfield, An American Impressionist, 1869-1965: The Redfield Letters, Vol. II, Lahaska, Pennsylvania, 2002, p. 404, no. 305, illustrated (as Winter at the Farm).James M. Alterman, New Hope for American Art, Lambertville, 2005, p. 446, illustrated.Lot Note:By the mid-1930s, Edward Redfield had spent more than three decades making the stone farmhouses, barns, and snowbound lanes of Bucks County the defining subject of Pennsylvania Impressionism. Winter on the Farm (Farbotnik Farm) is a later, yet no less assured statement of that endeavor. The farm, located in Solebury Township, belongs to the working agrarian landscape that Redfield and his New Hope-area contemporaries found just beyond their own doorsteps, and that they treated as a subject matter worthy of monumental canvases rather than as a mere backdrop. Here, the scene is built from the vernacular elements Redfield made his own: a weathered red barn, a snow-laden stone house with a single lit window, a cast-iron pump, and a farmer leading a horse through the drifts. Redfield, famously committed to finishing his large canvases outdoors in a single sustained session, renders the falling snow in a flurry of loaded, directional strokes of impasto. The tonal harmony of buff, slate, and umber is warmed by the barn's russet and the glow in the farmhouse windows, which gives the picture its quiet domestic note. Painted when Redfield was nearly 70 years old, the work shows no loss of command. The brushwork is as vigorous as in his earlier efforts, but the mood is arguably more reflective–a seasoned painter's affectionate record of a way of rural life he had chronicled, and in some sense helped to preserve, for a lifetime.
provenance: Jim’s of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey. Acquired from the above, 2004.

description_block:
Kenneth R. Nunamaker
(American, 1890-1957)
After the Fog, New Hope
oil on canvas
signed K. NUNAMAKER (lower right); bears artist's stamp (on the stretcher) 

22 x 24 in. 

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance: Christie's, New York, sale of May 28, 1992, Lot 192. Exhibited: Doylestown, Pennsylvania, James A. Michener Museum Art Museum, Earth River and Light: Masterworks of Pennsylvania Impressionism, September 21, 2002 – December 29, 2002 (and traveling to Florence Griswold Museum, Old Lyme, Connecticut, June 28 – September 28, 2003). Lot Note:Kenneth Nunamaker is best known for the sunstruck hillsides, stone houses, and rolling farmland of Bucks County, which makes After the Fog, New Hope an unusual yet quietly rewarding work. The subject is the Delaware at winter's edge, with broken ice plates stacked along the near shore and open, slate-blue water moving beyond them. A bank of bare, russet-toned trees leans in at the left and dissolves into the haze, while the far side of the river disappears altogether. The palette is limited to pearl gray, pale buff, and steel blue, and the paint is applied in flat, deliberate planes, so that the ice reads as a faceted, almost architectural surface. With no horizon line to speak of and no figure or building to give scale, the picture depends on tonal control rather than incident. That restraint gives After the Fog, New Hope a measured, almost documentary character. Here, the interest lies in observation–in the slow, quiet moment when weather lifts and the river's condition is revealed.
provenance: Christie's, New York, sale of May 28, 1992, Lot 192.

sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
George William Sotter
(American, 1879-1953)
Mill-Spring Valley
oil on masonite
signed G. W. Sotter (lower right); titled (on the reverse) 

21 3/8 x 25 1/4 in. 

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance:Rago Auctions, Lambertville, New Jersey, sale of April 30, 2005, Lot 98. Acquired from the above sale.Lot Note:George Sotter understood the poetry of winter darkness as profoundly as any painter of his generation, and Mill-Spring Valley is a testament to that understanding. Here, the Bucks County landscape is transformed by moonlight into a world of glacial greens and cobalt shadows, the snow-laden fields rendered in muscular strokes that seem to hold the cold light itself. A fieldstone mill, its roofline capped with snow, anchors the composition, while a modest arched bridge and the faint curve of a frozen stream draw the eye across the middle distance. Sotter's nocturnes are distinguished by their warmth amid the chill, and nowhere is this more evident than in the small, amber-lit windows that glow from the farmhouses beyond. These pinpoints of domestic life, set against a sky pricked with stars, lend the scene a quiet intimacy: a village at rest, sheltered beneath the hills.Trained in Pittsburgh and a longtime resident of Holicong, Pennsylvania, Sotter absorbed the Impressionist lessons of the New Hope School while forging a sensibility entirely his own. His nocturnes, born of long, patient observation of the Delaware Valley's fieldstone architecture and its changing light, occupy a singular place within American Tonalism's late flowering. They recall the poetic reverie of earlier masters, yet their robust, tactile surfaces and bold chromatic structure place them firmly in the twentieth century. In Mill-Spring Valley, the tracks of a wagon road sweep through the foreground snow in sinuous, rhythmic lines, while the bare, silvery birch in the left foreground, its trunk catching the pale glow, acts as a graceful repoussoir. The result is a work of remarkable balance and atmosphere, at once a faithful portrait of a place and a meditation on silence, endurance, and the consoling presence of home. Sotter's finest moonlit canvases are rarely so complete in their command of mood, so secure in their design, or so controlled in their palette.
provenance: Rago Auctions, Lambertville, New Jersey, sale of April 30, 2005, Lot 98. Acquired from the above sale.

Peterson, Up the River: The Pennsylvania Impressionists and Modernists, Princeton, 2001, p. 20, illustrated, also illustrated on the cover.Brian H. Peterson, Pennsylvania Impressionism, Philadelphia, 2002, p. 134, no. 46, illustrated.James M. Alterman, New Hope for American Art, Lambertville, 2005, p. 165, illustrated.Lance Humphries, Daniel Garber: Catalogue Raisonné, New York, 2006, vol. II, p. 148, no. P412, illustrated.Lot Note:From a terraced vantage on the Delaware, Daniel Garber looks across the river to the village of Stockton, New Jersey, with the unhurried authority of an artist wholly at home in his subject. In the foreground, a handful of figures in summer whites drift across a sunlit lawn, their croquet game casting long shadows over the grass. Beyond them the river shimmers in bands of lavender and silvered blue, and on the far bank the village rises in a patchwork of tile roofs, whitewashed gables, and a single slender spire. The landscape then climbs in tiers of meadow and woodland to a pearly, cloud-laden sky. It is a composition of calibrated recession, in which Garber leads the eye from the deep greens of the near foliage to the cool distant ridgeline. The figures are tiny and incidental, yet they animate the scene with an easy sociability, a reminder that this is a landscape inhabited and enjoyed as well as observed.Painted at the height of Garber's maturity, Stockton combines the dappled, broken touch of French Impressionism with the structural rigor he absorbed as a student, and later taught for four decades, at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. Houses and trees are built up from patches of pure, luminous color without ever dissolving into mere atmosphere, so that the view feels both observed and composed, shimmering yet secure. Garber's Delaware River Valley pictures are widely regarded as the pinnacle of his achievement, and Stockton is among the most poised and resolved of them. Nothing here is overstated; the painting's authority lies in the confidence with which Garber lets a quiet summer afternoon stand for an entire way of life along the river.

description_block:
Daniel Garber
(American, 1880-1958)
The Studio, 1922
oil on board
signed Daniel Garber (lower right); signed again and titled (on the reverse)

20 x 18 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Housed in a Frederick Harer frame.Provenance:The Artist.Grand Central Galleries, New York.Private Collection, Chicago (possibly Edward Burgess Butler), acquired from the above, July 1923.The Estate of Edward Burgess Butler, Chicago.Sotheby’s, New York, sale of May 18, 2005, Lot 58.Acquired from the above sale.Jim’s of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey, Acquired from the above, 2005.Exhibited:Philadelphia, Art Club of Philadelphia, Exhibition of Oil Paintings by Daniel Garber, Robert Henri, Frederick J. Waugh, November 18 – December 10, 1922, no. 39.New York, Macbeth Gallery, Recent Landscapes by Daniel Garber, N.A., January 2 – 22, 1923, no. 6.Doylestown, James A. Michener Art Museum, The Painterly Voice of Bucks County's Fertile Ground, October 22 - April 1, 2012.Literature:James M. Alterman, New Hope for American Art, Lambertville, 2005, p. 169, illustrated.Lance Humphries, Daniel Garber: Catalogue Raisonné, New York, 2006, vol. I, pp. 116-117; 166, illustrated, and vol. II, p. 163, no. P449, illustrated.Lot Note:In the best of Garber's work, the landscape of southeastern Pennsylvania is less a place than a luminous condition. In the present lot, he brings that condition indoors. In the Studio is dominated by a vast gridded window, its mullions laid across the canvas like a loose trellis, through which a wall of summer foliage presses toward the viewer in short, flickering strokes of viridian, sap green and lemon. Garber lets the warm buff of the ground breathe through this broken touch, so the whole surface shimmers with a dry, pastel-like vibration. The leaves seem to tremble in the heat. The effect is closer to the optical vibrancy of Post-Impressionist color than to the tempered Impressionism for which Garber is usually praised, and it is a reminder of how freely he could handle paint when the subject released him from the demands of a finished exhibition landscape.Against this green incandescence, Garber arranges a quiet drama of attention. At left, two women lean toward one another over a table, absorbed in some small task, while a potted plant and a leaning panel anchor the corner. At right, a seated figure bends toward a drawing board and a standing figure in a pale smock faces an easel streaked with violet and vermilion, her back turned entirely to us. The picture gives us the studio as a place of work and concentration, and the figures are built from the same dry, directional strokes as the foliage, so that room and garden dissolve into one another. A bouquet of wildflowers in a blue vase supplies the composition's sharpest chromatic accent, and the ochre and rust of the carpet in the foreground grounds the cool architecture of light above it. It is an interior that is also, quite deliberately, a landscape, and a rare and ambitious meeting of the two genres in Garber's oeuvre.The picture's early history reflects the esteem in which it was held. Shown at the Art Club of Philadelphia in the winter of 1922 alongside Robert Henri and Frederick Judd Waugh, and again at Macbeth Gallery in January 1923, it passed through Grand Central Galleries that July to a Chicago collection, possibly that of Edward Burgess Butler, in whose estate it remained until it first appeared at auction in 2005. Its inclusion in the James A. Michener Art Museum's 2012 exhibition on Bucks County painting confirmed its place within the region's canon. Presented in a handsome Harer frame, In the Studio is an unusually fresh and tactile work, accompanied by a distinguished record of exhibition and ownership.

description_block:
Walter Elmer Schofield
(American, 1867-1944)
After the Storm (Cornish Cove), c. 1941
oil on canvas
signed Schofield (lower left); titled (on the reverse)

26 x 30 in.
We are grateful to James Church, PhD, author of the forthcoming catalogue raisonné of Walter Elmer Schofield's works, for his assistance with cataloguing the present lot.Lot Note:Walter Elmer Schofield holds a singular place among the Pennsylvania Impressionists. A Philadelphia native trained at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, he moved to England and, by 1903, had discovered in the Cornish coast one of his defining subjects. After the Storm (Cornish Cove) reveals that transatlantic synthesis at its most vigorous. From a high promontory, the eye drops across sun-struck headlands of ochre, acid green, and violet shadow to a churning cove where the retreating surf breaks into flecks of white against silvered blue. The cliffs are built from short, broken strokes of thick impasto, so that the rock seems to flicker in the light, while the sea is laid in with a quicker, more dancing touch. The title is apt: the tumult has passed, and the world is rinsed and glittering. After the Storm (Cornish Cover) has the structural confidence that separates Schofield from his more decorative contemporaries, and reminds viewers that the reach of New Hope Impressionism extended far beyond the Delaware Valley.

sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
George William Sotter
(American, 1879-1953)
Windy Day, Cape Ann
oil on masonite
signed G. W. Sotter (lower right)

26 x 32 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Lot Note:Sotter is identified so closely with the rural villages and moonlit snowfields of Bucks County that Windy Day, Cape Ann offers a welcome counterpoint. The subject is the Massachusetts coast, and the picture turns on a contrast between the two halves of the canvas. Below the horizon, russet ledges tilt steeply into the foreground, their faceted planes picked out in ochre and rust, while the water breaks around them in cold teal and bottle green, flecked with quick strokes of white. Above, the sky takes up well over half the picture, and Sotter gives it his full attention. Great bands of cloud, violet at their undersides and creamy at their crests, sweep across the canvas in long, directional strokes, parting just above the horizon to admit a low seam of pale light. Against that opening, a schooner and a scattering of smaller sails stand out as slight silhouettes, which measures the scale of the weather overhead.The nocturnes for which Sotter is best known depend on enclosure–on the sheltering hill and the lit window. In Windy Day, Cape Ann the view is open and the light is mutable, and the eye is sent out to sea rather than drawn in toward a hearth. Even so, the picture shows the same habits at work: a firmly built composition, a palette organized around a few related hues, and an assured touch that lets the paint describe rock and cloud alike. Cape Ann, with its granite shoreline and its long tradition as a gathering place for American painters, held a lasting attraction for Sotter, and the canvas shows an artist applying his command of color and structure to a coast he had come to know intimately.

description_block:
John Fulton Folinsbee
(American, 1892-1972)
Salmon Weir
oil on canvas
signed John Folinsbee (lower left)

33 7/8 x 50 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance:Collection of Mr. James Murphy.Acquired from the above.Lot Note:With its rocky shoreline and uneven, seemingly untamed terrain, Maine drew artists such as Edward Redfield, who began summering in Boothbay Harbor in 1903 and later bought a house on Monhegan Island. Maine became Folinsbee's primary focus in the 1950s, after he purchased Murphy's Corner, an old farmhouse near Woolwich overlooking Montsweag Bay. Although he lacked Redfield's physical agility, he captured the raw beauty of the coast with vivid, dynamic brushwork, working either from land or at sea. The latter became possible once he bought a lobster boat, Sketch, which allowed him to approach the water with less difficulty and to record its transient nature from different perspectives.The present landscape offers a bird's-eye view of the open sea, most likely off Seguin Island, where a salmon weir extends diagonally between the shore and a small island at the center of the composition. In smooth, fluid strokes of dark green, blue, and white, Folinsbee suggests the strong wind that sweeps the region and drives the water against the shore, giving the picture a theatrical energy. As Kristen Jensen notes, "Folinsbee saw in the water what Homer, George Bellows, Robert Henri, and countless others saw—a challenge to transfer onto the still canvas the essence of movement, of something undergoing constant transformation not only volumetrically, but also tonally and in the way the light reflects off its ever-changing surface."

sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
Edward Willis Redfield
(American, 1869-1965)
Winter in New Hope
oil on canvas
signed E. W. REDFIELD (lower right)

26 x 32 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Provenance: Jim's of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey. Lote Note:Few painters have claimed a place so completely as Edward Redfield claimed the Delaware River Valley. In Winter in New Hope, the artist turns his attention to the village center, where the fieldstone farmhouses and clapboard dwellings of the old river town cluster along a snow-covered lane. The scene is quiet, but nothing in it is static. A team of draft horses stands harnessed to a green sleigh while two men tend to its load, and a small child in a bright green cap waits beside a discarded red sled. The glimpses of habitation (a wreath hung on a doorway, a porch hung with the stuff of daily life, a lone figure moving along the fence line) give the composition a warmth that its cool palette might otherwise deny. Redfield rarely needed a grand subject. His genius lay in recognizing that a working village on an ordinary winter morning contained everything a painter required.The painting's handling rewards close looking. Redfield, famous for completing his large canvases in a single sustained session out of doors, executes the snow in confident, buttery ribbons of white, cream, and lavender-blue, their ridges catching the light and describing every rut and drift of the roadway. Against this the leafless trees rise in a web of calligraphic strokes, their dark armatures set against a turquoise sky that lends the whole scene its crystalline chill. Raking light sets the yellow and rose facades aglow, a counterpoint of warm and cool that is the hallmark of the artist's finest winter subjects. Redfield was the most vigorous exponent of New Hope Impressionism and his snow scenes remain the benchmark by which the movement is measured. This work, with its balanced, animated composition and its fully resolved surface, captures the painter at the height of his powers and the village at its most picturesque.
provenance: Jim's of Lambertville, Lambertville, New Jersey.

Edward Willis Redfield
(American, 1869-1965)
Spring Veil, c. 1928
oil on canvas
signed E. W. Redfield (lower right); signed again and titled Edward W. Redfield/Spring Vale (on label affixed to the stretcher)

50 1/4 x 56 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
The present work will be included in the forthcoming catalogue raisonné of Edward Redfield's works being compiled by Dr. Thomas Folk.Housed in a Frederick Harer frame.Provenance:The Artist.The Estate of the Artist, no. 74.By decent to her daughter, Elise Hume. McClees Galleries, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania.Acquired from the above.Collection of Eleanor and Malcom Polis (Plymouth Meeting Gallery), Plymouth Meeting, Pennsylvania.Acquired from the above, November 2008.Exhibited:Washington D.C., The Corcoran Gallery of Art, Twelfth Biennial Exhibition of Contemporary American Oil Paintings, November 30, 1930 – January 11, 1931 (as Spring Veil).Philadelphia, Newman Galleries, A Retrospective Exhibition of the Work of Edward Redfield, October 23 – November 30, 1968.Bucks County Conservancy, A Retrospective Exhibition, June 19 – July 6, 1975.Allentown, Pennsylvania, Allentown Art Museum, Edward Willis Redfield: First Master of the Twentieth Century Landscape, September 20, 1987 – January 10, 1988 (and traveling to The Butler Institute of American Art, Youngstown, Ohio, February 14 – April 2, 1988).Doylestown, Pennsylvania, James A. Michener Art Museum, Masterworks of American Impressionism: Edward Redfield and the New Hope Group, March 26 – September 4, 1994.Doylestown, Pennsylvania, James A. Michener Art Museum, Earth, River and Light: Masterworks of Pennsylvania Impressionism, September 21 – December 29, 2002 (as Spring Vale).Doylestown, Pennsylvania, James A. Michener Art Museum, The Painterly Voice: Bucks County’s Fertile Ground, October 22, 2011 – April 1, 2012 (as Spring Vale).Literature:John M. W. Fletcher, Edward Willis Redfield (1869-1965), An American Impressionist: His Paintings and the Man Behind the Palette, Lahaska, Pennsylvania, 1996, p. 82, fig 13, illustrated (as Spring Vale) and p. 182, no. 705 (as Spring Vale c. 1925).John M. W. Fletcher, Edward Willis Redfield, An American Impressionist 1869-1965: The Redfield Letters, Vol. II, Lahaska, Pennsylvania, 2000, p. 398, no. 234, illustrated.Thomas Folk, Edward Redfield: First Master of the Twentieth Century Landscape, exhibition catalogue, Allentown Art Museum, Allentown, Pennsylvania, 1987, p. 72, no. 17, illustrated.Brian H. Peterson, Pennsylvania Impressionism, Philadelphia, 2002, p. 212, no. 127, illustrated.Lot Note:In 1898, Edward Redfield and his wife moved from Glenside, Pennsylvania to the Belle Island Farm in Centre Bridge, just five miles north of New Hope, along the Delaware River and canal. The bucolic region became the artist's most favored subject; one he captured every season from his studio in Point Pleasant. In a 1929 interview, the artist confessed the region’s powerful, almost mystical, hold over him: "There is a real 'church': go there at sundown and watch the changing colors in earth and sky and water. It is a place to worship."Of all the vistas Redfield produced, his Spring scenes appear amongst the most powerful, and sought-after works, as evidenced by Spring Veil, one of the largest canvases Redfield ever painted–a mythical oil largely reproduced and exhibited, which Redfield liked so much that he kept it his entire life.Executed en plein air, or outdoors, in "one go," for about seven continuous hours, Spring Veil depicts in thick and short brushstrokes a plunging view of the Delaware River in full bloom. The scene abounds with brightness and life. Redfield's familiarity with landscape painting, the large scale of the canvas, paired with his bold and swift application of paint through colorful and contrasting hues, are able to convey the bursting and reinvigorating feeling of spring, and tempt the viewer to walk right into the picture plane and enjoy the warmth of a peaceful, sunny day. Redfield started to paint his first spring scenes in Point Pleasant in the 1910s. Contrary to earlier canvases of the same subject such as Spring at Point Pleasant on the Delaware Valley (sold at Freeman’s on June 14, 2020) which incorporated picturesque details of Bucks County’s rural daily life such as a farmer, or animals, the present work seems to make spring its sole subject, so lush, abundant and luscious that the main tree at center–the true vertical of the entire composition–obstructs much of the view of the downtown habitations and river, barely noticeable through touches of turquoise spread out across the horizon line. Here, Redfield attains maturity, and puts his vigorous impasto to the service of the painting, which becomes less narrative but gains in expressivity, and bravura. The artist composes an all-surface pattern that enhances the immediacy of the scene, prompting the viewer to lose sight of its specific facts and instead dive into a mesmerizing abstract composition–one of the artist's boldest and more modern depictions of spring. In doing so, Redfield imbues the canvas with his own personality and charisma–a masculine energy that impressed his peers as much as it stunted them, and which he puts at the service of the greater American Art, making Spring Veil a perfect example of what a real American landscape, miles away from the western canyons and mountain ranges, can look and feel like: grand, serene, and bold.

sale_title: Pride of Place: Works from the Estate of Sydney F. and Sharon B. Martin – Part II
description_block:
Mary Elizabeth Price
(American, 1877-1965)
Still Life with Lillies and Foxgloves
oil with silver leaf on panel
signed M ELIZABETH PRICE (lower left) 

26 x 20 in.

This lot is located in Philadelphia.
Lot Note:Mary Elizabeth Price builds Still Life with Lilies and Foxgloves on a ground of silver leaf and allows the metal do the work that depth and atmosphere would do in a conventional still life. Lilies in ochre and olive-gold and foxglove spikes hung with bells of madder and plum rise from a dense thicket of strap-like leaves. Each form is fixed by a firm, dark contour and filled with thinly worked color. The blossoms are pressed against the picture plane and layered like the motifs of a textile or a screen, while the pale metal shows through between and beneath them, its sheen softened and broken by age. At the margins, a wash of lilac gives way to the cooler field behind. The garden is seen as pattern, with the vertical thrust of the foxgloves answered by the looping arcs of the foliage below.Price belonged to a generation of Philadelphia painters who absorbed Japanese decorative arts and the Arts and Crafts movement alongside Impressionism, and as a member of the Philadelphia Ten, the group of women artists who exhibited together as a collective and favored a more progressive, decorative idiom than the city's academic establishment, she pursued those interests with refreshing independence. Her use of silver leaf is the most individual part of her work. Here, the technique serves native garden flowers rather than exotic motifs. The contour drawing owes something to Japanese woodblock and screen traditions, and the oil is kept thin, in scumbled veils and economical strokes, so that the silver is never fully covered. The restrained palette of old gold, olive, wine, and mauve gives the panel its tension, and the drawing is confident enough to suggest the whole plant with a few lines. The picture is a distinctive example of the artist's work in metal leaf and a document of the decorative current in early twentieth-century American painting.
